questions.q: What is the correct bottom-to-top order of the OSI model's first four layers?
questions.explain: Bottom to top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application — remembered with "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away."

questions.q: A switch forwards traffic based on MAC addresses. Which OSI layer does a switch primarily operate at?
questions.explain: MAC addressing and frame forwarding are Data Link (Layer 2) functions — that's the layer switches operate at.

questions.q: Why does the OSI model remain useful even though no real network stack implements all seven layers exactly as described?
options: It's required by law for ISPs to use it
It gives engineers a shared vocabulary for localizing where a network problem actually lives
It's the only model that explains how Wi-Fi works
Real TCP/IP networks secretly do implement all seven layers
questions.explain: The OSI model's value is as a shared troubleshooting and design vocabulary — saying "it's a Layer 2 issue" conveys precise meaning even though TCP/IP doesn't map to it one-to-one.

questions.q: A user can ping their default gateway successfully but can't load any website. Which layer does this point to first?
options: Layer 1 (Physical) — the cable must be unplugged
Layer 2 (Data Link) — a duplicate MAC address
Layer 7 (Application) or above Layer 3 — since basic IP connectivity to the gateway already works, the problem is likely DNS or routing beyond the local network
This behavior is impossible and indicates a broken NIC
questions.explain: A successful ping to the gateway confirms Layers 1-3 are working locally, so the fault is most likely DNS resolution or routing further upstream, not a local physical or data-link issue.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for end-to-end delivery between two specific applications, using port numbers?
questions.explain: Layer 4 (Transport) handles end-to-end delivery between applications using port numbers, via TCP or UDP.
